title: Understanding Explicit Memory
header: Explore the hidden process your brain uses to store facts and life moments
content:
Understanding Memory: A Simple Guide

Memory is the process where your brain takes in information, stores it, and brings it back when you need it.

You have three main kinds of memory:

  • Sensory memory: What you sense right now. It lasts only seconds.
  • Short-term memory: Holds information for less than a minute unless repeated.
  • Long-term memory: Stores information for days, years, or even a lifetime.

Explicit memory is a type of long-term memory that helps you remember facts and events. It requires conscious recall. For example, if someone asks, “What is the capital of France?” you consciously search your memory for the answer: Paris.

Types of Explicit Memory

Explicit memory has two parts: semantic memory and episodic memory.

  • Semantic memory: General knowledge and facts.
  • Episodic memory: Personal experiences and events.

Examples of Explicit Memory

Semantic memory helps you:

  • Know that a “boat” is a type of watercraft.
  • Remember that Washington, D.C., is the capital of the United States.
  • Recognize what makes an animal a dog.

Episodic memory helps you:

  • Recall a trip you took with friends.
  • Remember a delicious meal at your favorite restaurant.
  • Think back to your high school graduation day.

How Long-Term Memories Are Made

Long-term memories form in three main steps:

1. Encoding

Your senses collect information and send it to the brain. You may process it lightly (appearance, size) or deeply (meaning, connections).

2. Storage

The brain stores encoded memories. Different parts of a memory can be stored in different brain regions. For example, visual details are stored in areas related to vision.

3. Retrieval

This is recalling stored information. Retrieval often needs a cue, like a question or reminder. Sometimes recall is easy, and sometimes it takes effort.

Explicit Memory vs. Implicit Memory

Long-term memory has two main types: explicit and implicit.

  • Explicit memory: You consciously recall information.
  • Implicit memory: Works unconsciously and influences your actions.

An example of implicit memory is driving a car — your body automatically knows how much pressure to put on the pedals, even if you can’t fully explain it.

How to Improve Long-Term Memory

These tips may help boost your memory and reduce memory loss:

  • Get enough sleep: Sleep strengthens memory. Review important information before bed.
  • Avoid multitasking: Splitting your attention makes it harder to store new memories.
  • Stay active: Exercise increases blood flow to the brain. Aim for regular movement, even short walks.
  • Challenge your mind: Do puzzles, learn skills, or play memory games.
  • Eat a healthy diet: Choose foods like leafy greens and fatty fish.
  • Stay organized: Use to-do lists, notes, and summaries to help reinforce learning.

The Bottom Line

Explicit memory helps you recall facts and personal experiences. It relies on conscious recall and plays a major role in your daily life.
author: Timothy J. Legg

title: Positive thinking vs negative thinking
header: Learn how to shift from negative thoughts to a healthier, happier mindset
content:
Positive Thinking vs Negative Thinking

Humans have the power to think, plan, and make decisions. Our thoughts shape our mood, our actions, and the quality of our lives. In general, people tend to fall into two groups:

  • Positive thinkers
  • Negative thinkers

Positive Thinkers

Positive thinkers look for the good in situations. They encourage others instead of discouraging them. Positive thinking doesn’t mean ignoring problems — it means facing challenges with a hopeful and productive mindset.

Positive thinking often starts with self-talk, the thoughts that run through your mind every day. These thoughts can be helpful or unhelpful. Some come from logic, while others come from fear or misunderstandings.

The Power of Positive Thinking

Positive thinking is a mindset that focuses on the good in life and expects good results. A positive person believes they can overcome challenges and succeed.

More people today believe in the power of positive thinking, and many books and courses teach this skill. But knowing about positive thinking is not enough — you must practice it daily.

Benefits of Positive Thinking

Positive thinking can improve your physical and emotional health in many ways:

  • Boosts immunity: Stress weakens your immune system. Positivity helps your body fight illness.
  • Improves heart health: Positive people tend to have lower stress and healthier habits.
  • Fights stress: Positivity reduces the harmful effects of long-term stress.
  • Increases resilience: Positive people recover from difficult situations more quickly.
  • May extend lifespan: Studies show that positive seniors live healthier, longer lives.
  • Helps tolerate pain: Positivity can reduce pain sensitivity and improve coping.
  • Encourages healthy habits: Positive people often exercise, sleep well, and eat nutritious foods.
  • Reduces hypertension: Positivity may help lower blood pressure.

Other Emotional Benefits

  • Better problem-solving
  • More enjoyment in life
  • Healthier habits
  • Higher self-esteem
  • More positive relationships

What Positive Thoughts Do to Your Brain

Research shows that positive emotions like joy and contentment open your mind and help you see more possibilities. People experiencing positive emotions come up with more ideas and more solutions than those feeling fear or anger.

Negative Thinkers

Negative thinkers focus on problems, mistakes, or what could go wrong. They often look for flaws instead of opportunities.

Common forms of negative thinking include:

  • Filtering: You focus only on the negative and ignore the positive.
  • Personalizing: You blame yourself for things that aren’t your fault.
  • Catastrophizing: You expect the worst outcome.
  • Polarizing: You see things as all good or all bad.

Physical Symptoms of Negative Thinking

  • Muscle tension and pain
  • Headaches
  • Chest discomfort
  • Low libido
  • Sleep problems
  • Digestive issues
  • Fatigue

Emotional Symptoms

  • Mood swings
  • Anxiety
  • Irritability
  • Depression
  • Lack of motivation

Behavioral Symptoms

  • Changes in appetite
  • Substance use
  • Social withdrawal
  • Anger outbursts

How to Change Negative Thoughts to Positive Thoughts

  • Smile more: Smiling sends positive signals to the brain.
  • Practice yoga or meditation: These help you become aware of your self-talk.
  • Replace negative thoughts consciously: For each negative thought, think of two positive ones.
  • Take control of your choices: Stop feeling like a victim. Decide how you want to respond.
  • Surround yourself with positive people: Positivity is contagious.
  • Help others: Supporting someone else can lift your mood.
  • Sing: Singing boosts mood and reduces stress.
  • Read or listen to positive content: Books, quotes, and podcasts can reinforce positivity.
  • Make gratitude lists: Write down what you’re thankful for when stress rises.

Positive Thinking Is a Skill

Changing your mindset takes time. But the more you practice positive thinking, the easier it becomes. Eventually, positivity becomes your natural way of thinking.

Positive and Negative Thinking Are Contagious

Your attitude affects others, and their attitude affects you. People naturally avoid negativity and are drawn to positive, uplifting individuals.

How to Build a Positive Mindset

  1. Learn about positivity and practice it daily.
  2. Ignore negative opinions from others about your growth.
  3. Visualize positive outcomes.
  4. Use positive words in your self-talk.
  5. Smile more often.
  6. Replace negative thoughts with positive ones every time they appear.
  7. Be patient — mindset change takes time.
  8. Expect good results and trust the process.
  9. Use affirmations to strengthen positive thinking.

With practice and persistence, you can shift your thinking, improve your emotional health, and create a happier life.
author: Dr Israt Hossain

title: How Much Do You Value Yourself?
header: Explore simple mindset shifts that turn self-doubt into self-value
content:
Stop Comparing Yourself and Start Valuing Yourself

Many people, especially women, compare themselves to others and end up doubting their worth. Thoughts like “Am I good enough?”, “Am I worthy?”, or “Do I look young enough?” can slowly damage self-esteem.

This becomes a cycle: we compare → we feel bad → we beat ourselves up → we compare again. We always think someone else has more money, success, beauty, luck or happiness.

Constant comparison lowers self-worth. Sometimes we even confuse self-worth with net worth, which makes things worse.

Society also pushes unrealistic standards — perfect bodies, perfect careers, perfect lives. Many people end up feeling inadequate or pressured to live a life that isn’t truly theirs.

Maybe you took a job you didn’t want because you felt pressured. Maybe you stayed in a relationship longer than you should have because leaving felt scary. These choices slowly drain your confidence and happiness.

It’s time to stop this cycle. Take a moment to notice your self-talk. Are you gentle and kind to yourself? Or harsh and judgmental?

We accept the love we think we deserve. So ask yourself: what limits have you placed on your own worth?

Sometimes we forget how amazing we truly are. Self-love may feel unfamiliar, but it is important. You must take care of your own needs first — only then can you care for others effectively.

Tip #1

Think of qualities you admire in others. Then notice how you already show those same qualities yourself — even if you never realized it.

Tip #2

Watch your thoughts. Ask yourself: “Would I say this to my best friend?” If not, don’t say it to yourself either.

You have many strengths. Imagine how different life would feel if you truly valued yourself.

Tip #3

Make a simple list of things that make you valuable:

  • I am there for my family.
  • I have a great sense of humour.
  • I am a good cook.

If this feels hard, ask someone you trust what they value about you. You might be surprised by what they see. When you value yourself, others will value you more too.

Self-worth is a daily practice. Become your own best friend. Treat yourself with kindness, care, compassion, and patience — because you deserve it.

Give yourself the gift of time. Taking breaks from daily stress can inspire you, motivate you, and rebuild your self-worth.

title: How Hugs Can Help with Stress and Anxiety?
header: Learn why a hug may be the easiest mental health tool you’re missing
content:
How Hugs Help Reduce Stress and Anxiety

When we feel stressed or anxious, we often look for comfort. Some people listen to music, some exercise, and others meditate. But there is a simple and powerful way to feel better — hugs.

Hugging is a natural way humans give and receive comfort. Studies show that hugs release oxytocin, a “feel-good” hormone that helps reduce stress and anxiety. Hugs make us feel calm, safe, and supported.

How Hugs Help Your Mental Health

  • 1. Hugs lower cortisol levels.
    Cortisol is the stress hormone. High cortisol can raise blood pressure and weaken the immune system. Hugging helps lower cortisol, reducing the negative effects of stress on the body.
  • 2. Hugs increase feelings of social support.
    Feeling supported is important for mental health. A simple hug can help you feel connected, cared for, and less alone. This support makes stress easier to handle.
  • 3. Hugs improve mood.
    Hugging releases endorphins — the body’s natural “happy hormones.” These hormones can lift your mood and help reduce anxiety and depression. A hug from someone you love can make a huge difference when you're feeling low.
  • 4. Hugs improve communication.
    A hug can create closeness and trust. When people feel connected, they communicate better and understand each other more easily. This can lower stress and reduce tension in relationships.

Hugs are simple, free, and effective. Whether it's from a friend, family member, or partner, a hug can bring comfort when you need it most.

Next time you feel stressed or anxious, consider asking for a hug — it might be exactly what your heart and mind need.

title: Psychology of Confirmation Bias
header: Unlock the hidden bias that makes you ignore facts and trust your own opinions
content:
What Is Confirmation Bias?

People often hold on tightly to their beliefs, even when there is clear evidence against them. In psychology, this is called confirmation bias. It is one of the most common cognitive biases we experience.

Confirmation bias happens when we only notice, remember, or believe information that supports what we already think. Most of us are unaware we are doing it. It is like having a small voice in our head that always agrees with us, even when the facts don’t.

This bias affects many everyday decisions. We tend to look for proof that matches our opinions and ignore anything that challenges them.

How Confirmation Bias Shows Up

1. How we search for information

The way we look for information can shape what we find. For example:

  • A scientist may design a study based on what they already believe, which can affect the results.
  • A lawyer may ask leading questions to guide a person toward a specific answer.
  • Social media “filter bubbles” show us posts that match our beliefs, making our views stronger over time.

If you believe in UFOs, for example, platforms like YouTube or Facebook will continue showing you more UFO content — reinforcing your belief.

2. How we interpret information

Even when two people see the same facts, they may reach opposite conclusions.

Example: A chart shows that a state with more gun control laws has fewer murders.

  • A person who supports gun control may say, “This proves gun laws reduce murders.”
  • A person against gun control may say, “This is just correlation, not proof.”

People often judge evidence that opposes their beliefs more harshly. They may ask for impossible levels of proof before accepting anything that contradicts their views.

3. How we remember information

This is sometimes called selective recall. We remember information that supports our beliefs and forget the rest.

Example: Couples often remember the same argument differently.

One says: “You were rude to my father.”
The other says: “I was just answering his questions.”

We remember things more strongly when they match our expectations or when we are emotional during the event.

What Can You Do About Confirmation Bias?

Since confirmation bias is unconscious, it cannot be removed completely. But you can reduce its impact by doing the following:

  • Challenge your own beliefs, especially the ones you feel strongly about.
  • Actively seek out different viewpoints and try to read them with an open mind.
  • Ask yourself: “What evidence would prove me wrong?”
  • Be curious, not defensive, when learning something new.

You may not eliminate confirmation bias fully, but becoming more aware of it can help you understand yourself better and make more balanced decisions.

title: Five Tips To A Better Sleep
header: Discover small nightly habits that can help you fall asleep faster and wake up refreshed
content:
5 Simple Ways to Sleep Better

Ilter Dumduz, founder of the wellness app Blys, shares five easy tips to help you get better sleep and feel more rested.

Sleep Awareness Week reminds us that sleep is just as important as a healthy diet and regular exercise. When we don’t sleep well, we may have trouble focusing, feel moody, and face a higher risk of health problems.

Life can be busy with work, family, and social plans, but small daily habits can make a big difference to your sleep.

1. Stay active and get sunlight

What you do during the day affects how well you sleep at night. Being active and getting sunlight helps keep your body clock (circadian rhythm) balanced.

  • Try to spend 30 minutes outside during lunch.
  • Go for a short morning walk or run.
  • If you work indoors, sit near a window or take calls while walking outside.

Like children, adults sleep better when they’ve moved their bodies and had sunlight during the day.

2. Unplug or reduce blue light

Blue light from phones and computers tells your brain it’s daytime. This lowers melatonin and makes it harder to relax before bed.

  • Put away devices at least 1–2 hours before bed.
  • Choose calming activities like reading or listening to a podcast.
  • If you must use screens, try apps that reduce blue light.

3. Watch what you eat before bed

Heavy meals before bedtime can make you uncomfortable and affect your sleep quality. Eating too much late at night can also reduce melatonin.

If you are hungry before bed, choose foods that support better sleep:

  • Nuts (walnuts, flax seeds, pumpkin seeds) – natural sedatives
  • Beans – high in vitamin B, help with insomnia
  • Dairy – contains sleep-supporting amino acids
  • Bananas – contain calming amino acids

4. Create a pre-sleep routine

A relaxing nightly routine helps your body and mind prepare for sleep. Try:

  • Meditation with apps like Headspace or Calm
  • A warm bath or shower before bed
  • Regular self-care habits that help calm your mind
  • Occasional massage to reduce anxiety and improve sleep

Apps like Blys allow you to book massages at home, which can be a helpful pre-sleep ritual.

5. Stay consistent with your sleep schedule

Going to bed and waking up around the same time helps regulate your body clock. This supports long-term sleep quality — even on weekends.

  • Set a nightly cut-off time for phone and internet use.
  • Use your phone’s “Bedtime” feature to track sleep and set reminders.
  • Keep your routine simple and repeat it daily.

Good sleep comes from small habits practiced consistently. Choose one or two tips to start with, and build your routine over time.

title: Get busy, be happy
header: Explore why meaningful work feels lighter even when you work harder
content:
Be Busy With What Matters

People often say that being busy makes us happy. Research from the University of Chicago shows that busy people feel happier, even when the task itself is pointless.

But is it really better to stay busy doing meaningless things? I’ve been there. I kept myself super busy with work that did not inspire me. Yes, I felt productive, but the happiness faded once I realised the work didn’t matter much.

However, when I worked on things that inspired me, I felt excited and full of energy. I could work just as hard, but it felt completely different.

If you really want to be happy, get busy doing the things that matter. Take inspired action toward your goals and dreams — even small steps count.

What is inspired action?

Inspired action is meaningful action. It is the kind of busyness that lights you up.

  • Do what you love.
  • Find something you enjoy in the work you already do.
  • Take pride in even the smallest task, knowing it is moving you closer to your dreams.

Sometimes all you need is to reframe the busyness. Life has dull moments, chores, and tasks we don’t enjoy.

For example, folding laundry might feel boring, but on good days, I see it as a way to support my family. Focusing on the meaning — not the annoyance — makes the task lighter.

Reframing also helps you see hidden opportunities. Years ago, I had a draining job. After months of frustration, I reframed it as a “Master Class” in what not to do. I learned from the good and the bad, and these lessons helped me later when I started my own writing business.

Be busy getting quiet

Sometimes inspired action means doing nothing. It means being still, sitting quietly, and making space for creativity.

This is hard because our culture rewards ambition and productivity. No one praises you for sitting still.

But when I spend part of my day being quiet, I feel happier, healthier, and less stressed. That quiet often reveals the next step I need to take.

When you don’t know what to do

If you’re unsure what your inspired action is, try doing something kind for someone else. Kindness boosts your mood, and with a positive mind, new ideas and opportunities appear more easily.

Why being busy feels good

  • We are built to create.
  • We are built to learn.
  • We are built to contribute.

So yes — being busy can make us happy. But being busy with something meaningful makes us even happier.

Inspired action moves you mentally, emotionally, and spiritually — and it inspires others too.
author: Polly Campbell

title: These Daily Habits Might Be Damaging Your Brain Health
header: Find out which common routines harm brain health and what to do instead
content:
10 Habits That Harm Your Brain Health and How to Avoid Them

Brain health is your brain’s overall well-being. It includes how well you think, remember, feel, and make decisions. Some daily habits can slowly damage your brain over time. Here are the habits to watch out for and simple ways to avoid them.

1. Lack of sleep

Not getting enough sleep hurts memory, focus, and overall brain function.

  • Follow a regular sleep schedule.
  • Have a calming bedtime routine.
  • Avoid caffeine and alcohol at night.
  • Keep your sleep environment cool and comfortable.

2. Poor nutrition

Unhealthy diets with too much sugar, saturated fat, and processed food may increase the risk of cognitive decline and dementia.

  • Eat fruits, vegetables, whole grains, nuts, and healthy fats.
  • Choose lean protein.
  • Drink enough water.
  • Reduce processed foods and sugar.

3. Sedentary lifestyle

Sitting too much reduces blood flow to the brain and affects memory and focus.

  • Walk, jog, cycle, or swim regularly.
  • Add strength and flexibility exercises.

4. Excessive stress

Chronic stress raises cortisol levels, which can damage the brain’s memory center (the hippocampus).

  • Practice deep breathing or meditation.
  • Try yoga or relaxing hobbies.
  • Take short breaks during the day.

5. Multitasking

Doing too many things at once can weaken focus and reduce memory.

  • Focus on one task at a time.
  • Prioritize your tasks.
  • Practice mindfulness.

6. Lack of mental stimulation

Not challenging your mind can lead to cognitive decline over time.

  • Read books or articles.
  • Do puzzles or brain games.
  • Learn a new skill or language.
  • Play music or engage in thoughtful conversations.

7. Excessive screen time

Too much screen time disrupts sleep, weakens focus, and reduces attention span.

  • Limit screen time when possible.
  • Take breaks every 20–30 minutes.
  • Spend more time outdoors.
  • Do hobbies without screens.

8. Isolation or loneliness

Low social interaction can increase the risk of cognitive decline and mental health issues.

  • Stay connected with friends and family.
  • Join groups, classes, or clubs.
  • Volunteer or participate in community activities.

9. Substance abuse

Alcohol, tobacco, and drugs damage brain cells and affect mental health.

  • Seek help if you struggle with addiction.
  • Use healthier coping methods.
  • Build a supportive social circle.

10. Neglecting mental health

Ignoring anxiety, depression, or chronic stress can harm your brain and daily functioning.

  • Seek help from a mental health professional.
  • Practice self-care.
  • Do activities that bring happiness.
  • Address stress early instead of ignoring it.

Healthy habits like eating well, exercising, sleeping enough, managing stress, and staying mentally active can help protect your brain and keep it strong for years to come.

title: Signs you’re avoiding your feelings
header: Learn how nonstop busyness may be avoiding feelings your mind needs to process
content:
Signs You Stay Busy to Avoid Your Emotions

Sometimes people stay busy so they don’t have to feel their emotions. These can also be early signs of depression. According to Dr. Bryant, here are the common signs to watch for:

  1. You stay busy every time you start to feel strong emotions.
  2. When you stop being busy, your emotions come back quickly and make you feel sad or hopeless.
  3. You feel easily angry, frustrated, short-tempered, or anxious.
  4. You don’t make time to slow down or take care of yourself.
  5. People around you ask if you’re okay or mention how busy you always are.

  8. You can’t remember the last time you checked in with your own feelings.

title: What does happiness look like to you?
header: Explore what truly brings happiness beyond money, likes, and success
content:
What Does Happiness Really Mean?

Is it money? Is it getting more likes or follows on Instagram? Is it a relationship?

It’s okay to want these things and work toward them. But how do we feel content while chasing our goals? Maybe happiness is not a destination at all.

Dr. Ryan T. Howell, Assistant Professor of Psychology at San Francisco University, said: “Happy people make decisions every day that improve their wellbeing.”

Happy people usually:

  • Manage their finances wisely
  • Spend money on experiences rather than material things
  • Look back on the past with warmth
  • Have healthy friendships and support systems

The best part? Happiness is something you can shape for yourself. You get to design the life you want.

My happiness list includes sunrise walks on the beach, watching disco balls reflect light around my home, sprinkles on desserts, and bubble baths.

What does your list say?

title: Endowment Effect: Definition, What Causes It, and Example
header: Learn how this mental bias quietly affects your buying, selling, and decisions
content:
What Is the Endowment Effect?

The endowment effect is an emotional bias where people value an item more just because they own it, even if its market value is lower.

Key Takeaways

  • People value things they already own more than things they do not own.
  • The effect is stronger for objects with emotional or symbolic meaning.
  • Ownership and loss aversion are the two main causes of the endowment effect.
  • Marketers often use this bias in selling and advertising strategies.
  • Investors can avoid this bias by following a clear plan for when to sell investments.

Understanding the Endowment Effect

In behavioral finance, the endowment effect (also called divestiture aversion) explains why people overvalue things they own. This can happen with items that have emotional meaning, but it can also happen simply because ownership itself increases perceived value.

Example of the Endowment Effect

Imagine someone buys an inexpensive case of wine. Later, the market price rises slightly. Even if selling the wine would give them a profit, the owner might refuse because owning it makes them see it as more valuable. They may wait for a higher offer—or drink it themselves.

This effect also appears with collectibles, personal belongings, or even businesses. Owners often feel their asset is more valuable than what the market says.

In rational choice theory, this is considered irrational. A rational person should value the wine at its current market price since they could buy a similar case for the same amount.

The Endowment Effect Triggers

  1. Ownership: People naturally value what they own more than similar items they don’t own. This happens whether the item was purchased or gifted.
  2. Loss aversion: People dislike losses more than they enjoy gains. This causes investors to hold on to losing assets because selling feels like a loss.

How Does the Endowment Effect Impact Buyers?

The effect influences buyers too. People may only be willing to sell an item at a high price but would refuse to buy the same item at that price. This creates a gap between buying prices and selling prices.

Why Is It Called the Endowment Effect?

The term was introduced by economist Richard Thaler. He used it to explain why people value goods that belong to their personal “endowment” more than goods outside of it.

What Is the Opposite of the Endowment Effect?

The opposite is called the reversed endowment effect. This happens when people prefer to get rid of an unwanted item and are willing to trade it for another unwanted item.

Is the Endowment Effect a Cognitive Bias?

Yes. It is a cognitive bias that changes how people see the value of things they already own. It is often irrational because two items of equal value may not be treated as equal.

The Bottom Line

The endowment effect explains why people value their own items more than similar items they do not own. This bias can lead to selling items at higher prices and buying at lower prices. Investors can reduce this bias by following a clear investment plan and having an exit strategy.
author: AKHILESH GANTI

title: How to Improve Your Self-Worth and Why It's Important
header: Unlock the hidden power of self-worth and how it shapes every area of your life
content:
What Is Self-Worth?

Self-worth is how you see yourself as a capable, valuable person who deserves love, respect, and care. It is your inner belief that you are worthy.

We often think of respect, love, and kindness in terms of how we treat others. But self-worth is about how much you respect, value, and love yourself.

People with high self-worth usually have better confidence and higher self-esteem. People with low self-worth tend to judge themselves harshly, focus on mistakes, and overlook their strengths.

Self-worth affects everything: your relationships, your work, your decisions, and how you feel about yourself.

Factors That Influence Self-Worth

Your sense of self-worth can change over time. These are some things that may affect it:

  • Your core beliefs and values
  • Your thoughts and feelings
  • Your emotional and mental health
  • Your life experiences
  • Your past and present relationships
  • Your physical health and fitness
  • Your work or career
  • Your hobbies
  • Your community and social status
  • Your financial situation
  • Your physical appearance
  • Your childhood experiences

How to Check Your Self-Worth

Ask yourself these questions to understand your self-worth:

  • How much do I like, respect, and value myself?
  • How would I describe myself to a stranger?
  • Are my thoughts about myself mostly positive or negative?
  • Do I believe I deserve love, respect, and kindness from others?

It can also help to reflect on where your beliefs about yourself originally came from.

Why Self-Worth Matters

Benefits of Positive Self-Worth

When you have healthy self-worth:

  • You feel confident that you can handle challenges.
  • You notice your strengths, not just your weaknesses.
  • You are more open to opportunities and growth.
  • You set healthy boundaries in relationships.
  • You do not blame yourself for others’ mistreatment.

People with good self-worth often feel happier and more satisfied with life.

Problems Linked to Low Self-Worth

Low self-worth can lead to:

  • Doubting your abilities
  • Fear of failure
  • Difficulty accepting compliments
  • Focusing on your flaws
  • Letting others ignore or cross your boundaries
  • Putting others above yourself

Low self-worth is also linked to anxiety and depression, which can cause:

  • Low mood or sadness
  • Irritability
  • Worry and anxiety
  • Fatigue
  • Sleep problems
  • Changes in appetite or weight
  • Trouble concentrating

How to Improve Your Self-Worth

  • Do things you enjoy and do well: Doing activities you are good at helps remind you of your strengths and boosts confidence.
  • Exercise and challenge yourself: Physical activity can improve your self-worth. Achieving small goals shows you that you are capable of more than you think.
  • Challenge negative thoughts: Thoughts are not always facts. When a negative thought appears, try replacing it with a more realistic and kinder one.
  • Seek support: If low self-worth affects your relationships, work, or emotions, therapy can help. A trained professional can help you see yourself more clearly.
  • Build self-worth in children: If you have children, help them develop healthy self-esteem by praising their effort, determination, and actions—not just their appearance or achievements.

A strong sense of self-worth supports better relationships, better mental health, and a more fulfilling life. If you struggle with low self-esteem, remember that change is possible. Treating yourself with love and respect can be the first step toward receiving the same from others.
author: Sanjana Gupta

title: The psychological reason most people overvalue things they already own
header: Find out how a hidden bias makes you think your stuff is worth more than it is
content:
The car's owner probably values it more than the buyer, thanks to a cognitive bias called the endowment effect.

Behavioral economists have shown that human behavior often deviates from standard economic theory. Our decisions are not always rational — they’re influenced by emotions and mental blind spots.

The endowment effect explains why we value things more once we own them. For example, I may think my car is worth $10,000, while you may think it’s only worth $7,000.

The endowment effect was first described by economist Richard Thaler in the 1970s. He shared the example of a man who bought wine for $5 a bottle in the 1950s. Years later, a merchant offered $100 per bottle. Even though the man had never paid more than $35 for wine, he refused to sell — simply because he owned it.

In 1990, Thaler, Daniel Kahneman, and Jack Knetsch published research that demonstrated this effect.

In their study, college students were randomly assigned to be sellers, buyers, or choosers. Sellers received a university mug and were asked how much money they needed to give it up. Buyers were asked how much they would pay for the mug. Choosers could pick between the mug or the same amount of cash at different price levels.

The results were clear:

  • Sellers wanted a median of $7.12 to part with the mug.
  • Choosers valued it at a median of $3.12.
  • Buyers were only willing to pay a median of $2.87.

So, what causes the endowment effect?

Behavioral economists first explained it through loss aversion. Losing something we own feels worse than gaining something new. Giving up a car we’ve had for years feels like a bigger loss than the gain of buying another car.

Later research suggests that possessions become connected to our identity. When something feels like part of us, it becomes harder to let go.

Whether you’re negotiating over a mug, a pen, or a car, being aware of the endowment effect can help. When you understand why an item feels valuable — to you or someone else — you can step back, think more clearly, and negotiate with better insight.

title: Overthinking: The Silent Saboteur of Happiness and How to Overcome It
header: Unlock the secret to stopping overthinking and reclaiming your peace, clarity, and confidence
content:
OVERTHINKING IS THE BIGGEST CAUSE OF UNHAPPINESS.

Many of us overanalyze, dwell on the past, or worry about the future. Overthinking can freeze us, feed self-doubt, and keep us from moving forward. If we don’t stop it, it becomes a major block to growth, peace, and happiness.

IT TOOK ME 9 YEARS TO BEAT OVERTHINKING.

Overcoming overthinking is possible. It takes patience, awareness, and the courage to challenge your thoughts. Here are simple but powerful ways to beat overthinking:

Avoid self-rejection

Overthinking often leads to rejecting yourself before anyone else can. Instead of doubting your abilities, take action. Apply for the opportunity. Share your work. Send the message. Don’t let fear make decisions for you. Growth comes from trying.

The power of now

Overthinking pulls you into the past or the future. The only moment you can control is the present. Focus on what you can do now. Let go of old regrets and future “what ifs.” The present moment is where change happens.

Fact-check your thoughts

Your mind can create stories based on fear, insecurity, or assumptions. Before believing a thought, ask: “Is this true?” Look for real evidence. This breaks the cycle of emotional thinking and helps you see situations more clearly.

Overthinking affects your peace, confidence, and happiness. By practicing these tools, you can slowly break the pattern and build a calmer, more balanced life. Take it one step at a time. Healing takes time, but with consistency and kindness toward yourself, you can overcome overthinking.

  • Fact-check your thoughts
  • Challenge negative stories your mind creates
  • Stay in the present moment
  • Avoid self-rejection

These simple habits can help you take back your power and live with more clarity and confidence.

Let go of the weight of overthinking and take the first step toward a lighter, brighter future — the future you truly deserve.

title: Simple and Natural Beauty TIPS Everyone Should Know
header: Unlock the Real Meaning of Happiness and Discover What Truly Makes Life Feel Good
content:
Whether you’re a makeup beginner or a beauty lover, there’s always something new to learn. Maybe you’ve mastered the perfect cat eye but struggle with hair styling. Or you can contour like a pro but can’t get your nail polish smooth. Below are 45 easy beauty tips from editors, experts and makeup artists that anyone can use.

Beauty Tip 1: Swap Regular Mascara for Waterproof

Waterproof mascara helps lashes hold a curl better — it acts like a “perm” that locks in the lift.

Beauty Tip 2: Ice Water Helps Nail Polish Dry Faster

After painting your nails, dip them into ice water to speed up drying time.

Beauty Tip 3: Use Powder to Make Lipstick Matte

Apply lipstick, place a tissue over your lips, and dust loose powder on top. This absorbs shine and turns any lipstick matte.

Beauty Tip 4: Store Makeup Wipes Upside Down

Flip your makeup wipes so the product soaks through every towelette — the top one stays fresh and moist.

Beauty Tip 5: Start Winged Liner at the Outer Corner

Draw the wing from the outer corner first, then fill it in. It’s easier than starting from the inner corner.

Beauty Tip 6: Use Tape to Catch Eyeshadow Fallout

Place tape under your eyes before applying heavy or glitter eyeshadow to catch fallout.

Beauty Tip 7: Make a DIY Lip Scrub

Mix coconut oil and brown sugar to exfoliate flaky lips before applying lipstick.

Beauty Tip 8: Sleep With an Extra Pillow

Keeping your head slightly raised helps reduce morning puffiness.

Beauty Tip 9: Cover Your Lids When Applying Mascara

Hold a spoon, card or tissue behind your lashes to prevent smudges on your eyelids.

Beauty Tip 10: Braid Hair Before Bed

Braid wet or dry hair at night to wake up with soft, beachy waves.

Beauty Tip 11: Spray Bobby Pins With Hairspray

Hairspray gives them extra grip. Wear them with the wavy side facing down.

Beauty Tip 12: Use Clear or White Lip Liner

It prevents lipstick from bleeding or smudging.

Beauty Tip 13: Mix Moisturizer With Foundation

This gives you a dewy glow and makes full-coverage foundation feel lighter and more natural.

Beauty Tip 14: Try the Connect-the-Dots Eyeliner Trick

Create small dots along your lash line, then connect them for an easy wing.

Beauty Tip 15: Don’t Wax or Thread Brows at Home

Stick to plucking — it’s safer and helps you avoid removing too much at once.

Beauty Tip 16: Wet Your Eyeshadow Brush With Setting Spray

This boosts pigment and makes the shadow last longer.

Beauty Tip 17: Use Clear Lip Balm to Groom Brows

Press a small amount into your brows to tame them quickly.

Beauty Tip 18: Layer Moisturizer With Face Oil

Apply face oil over moisturizer for extra hydration.

Beauty Tip 19: Apply Winged Liner With Eyes Open

Looking straight in the mirror helps you match both sides, especially if you have hooded eyes.

Beauty Tip 20: Try an At-Home Gel Polish Alternative

Gel-like polishes (like two-step systems) last long without UV lamps — just reapply top coat after a week.

Beauty Tip 21: Try the Cupid’s Bow Lip Liner Hack

This helps you shape your lips evenly and smoothly on the first try.

Beauty Tip 22: Use Two Elastics for a Fuller Ponytail

Stack two ponytails on top of each other to make your ponytail look longer and thicker.

Beauty Tip 23: Clean Mistakes With Micellar Water

Use a cotton swab dipped in micellar water to fix eyeliner or shadow errors.

Beauty Tip 24: Sleep on a Silk Pillowcase

Silk reduces frizz and is gentler on your hair than cotton.

Beauty Tip 25: Press Brows With Your Fingers

After applying brow gel, gently press hairs down so they stay in place.

Beauty Tip 26: Fix a Broken Nail With a Tea Bag

Use a piece of a tea bag as a patch under nail glue to reinforce the break.

Beauty Tip 27: Use Brown Eyeshadow for a Softer Smoky Eye

Brown looks less harsh and blends more naturally than black.

Beauty Tip 28: Tame Flyaways With a Spoolie

Spray a clean spoolie with hairspray and brush down flyaways.

Beauty Tip 29: Tightline Your Upper Waterline

This makes your lashes look thicker instantly.

Beauty Tip 30: Do Your Face Mask in the Shower

It saves time and helps ingredients absorb better.

Beauty Tip 31: Wear Socks Over Foot Mask Booties

This keeps them in place and lets you walk around easily.

Beauty Tip 32: Dry Hair With a Microfiber Towel

Microfiber or a soft T-shirt reduces frizz and prevents breakage.

Beauty Tip 33: Remove Dried Mascara Marks With a Brush

Once dry, flick mascara off gently using a clean fluffy brush.

Beauty Tip 34: Steady Your Hand for Cat Eye

Rest your hand under your chin to keep the line smooth and steady.

Beauty Tip 35: Use Concealer Instead of Foundation

Use different shades to highlight, contour, and spot-cover — great for a lighter makeup routine.

Beauty Tip 36: Remove Makeup Stains With a Makeup Wipe

Makeup wipes can quickly lift stains from clothes.

Beauty Tip 37: Sketch Your Wing With Pale Eyeshadow First

This helps you outline your shape before going in with real liner.

Beauty Tip 38: Prep Skin Before Makeup

Good makeup starts with exfoliating and hydrating your skin.

Beauty Tip 39: Always Wear Primer

Primer smooths texture, corrects skin issues, and helps your foundation last all day.

Beauty Tip 40: Stop Liner at the Midpoint

For beginners, lining only halfway across your lid elongates your eyes without needing a full line.

Beauty Tip 41: Take Time Finding the Right Shade

If you’re unsure of undertones, pick a neutral shade — it blends more naturally on most skin tones.

Beauty Tip 42: Use a Dense Brush for Foundation

A dense, flat or domed brush blends foundation without soaking up product like a sponge.

Beauty Tip 43: Try an Under-Eye Bags Treatment

Use a tightening treatment before makeup to temporarily smooth under-eye bags.

Beauty Tip 44: Always Wear Sunscreen

SPF is essential every day — even in winter.

Beauty Tip 45: Brighten Eyes With White Eyeliner

Apply white eyeliner on your lower waterline to brighten tired or red eyes.

title: Health Tips for Healthy Living
header: Learn the Everyday Health Habits Most People Ignore — But Your Body Needs
content:
This article gives simple tips to help you improve your daily habits and live a healthier lifestyle. It focuses on the major actions that support good health and also highlights some common habits to avoid.

“Healthy living” means having both physical and mental health in balance. Because the mind and body affect each other, improving one often improves the other. Some of the tips below support emotional and mental well-being too.

Healthy Eating (Diet and Nutrition)

Everyone needs food for growth and a healthy body. But nutrition needs change with age — infants, kids, teens, adults, and seniors all have different requirements. Eating patterns also differ; for example, young children often snack between meals, and many adults do too.

Tips:

  • Eat three healthy meals a day — breakfast, lunch, and dinner. Dinner does not need to be the largest meal.
  • Focus on fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and low-fat or fat-free dairy products.
  • Include lean meats, poultry, fish, beans, eggs, and nuts (especially beans and nuts).
  • Choose foods low in saturated fats, trans fats, cholesterol, sodium, and added sugars. Check labels — ingredients listed first are in the highest amounts.
  • Control portion sizes. Eat just enough to satisfy hunger, then stop.
  • Healthy snacks (fruit, whole grains, nuts) are okay in moderation.
  • Avoid sodas and sugary drinks. Even diet drinks can increase hunger for some people.
  • Avoid large meals before sleeping to help prevent reflux and weight gain.
  • Do not use food to cope with anger or sadness — it can make emotional stress worse.
  • Avoid rewarding children with sugary snacks to prevent unhealthy lifelong habits.
  • Avoid heavy meals during hot summer days.
  • Vegetarian diets can be healthy for weight control, but vegetarians should check with a doctor to ensure they get enough vitamins, minerals, and iron.
  • Cook foods above 165°F to kill bacteria. If eating raw fruits or vegetables, wash them well with safe running water.
  • Avoid eating raw or undercooked meats.

Tips for Special Situations:

  • People with diabetes should follow these tips and monitor glucose as directed. Keep blood sugar as close to normal as possible.
  • People with night shifts, students, or military schedules should still try to follow a breakfast–lunch–dinner routine with limited snacking.
  • When cooking, avoid frying or using excess grease.
  • People trying to lose weight should avoid fatty and sugary foods, focus on vegetables, fruits, and nuts, and limit meat and dairy intake.

Seek medical advice early if you struggle to manage your weight, your eating habits, or your blood glucose levels.

title: If You Want a Healthy Relationship, Value Yourself
header: Discover Why Loving Yourself First Transforms Love, Boundaries, and Happiness
content:
“It’s all about falling in love with yourself and sharing that love with someone who appreciates you, rather than looking for love to compensate for a self-love deficit.” ~ Eartha Kitt

I used to find the idea of self-love embarrassing and uncomfortable. It felt wrong and even selfish. Now I can see that my strong reaction came from not having self-love at all.

Because I didn’t love myself, many areas of my life suffered — especially my romantic relationships. I wanted someone to make me feel loved, safe, and happy. I depended on my partners to “fix” my feelings, and when I felt bad, I blamed them.

Without knowing it, I expected others to give me what I was not giving myself — worth, validation, attention, and love. This led to codependency, resentment, and constant disappointment.

Over time, while healing from codependency, I learned powerful lessons about self-worth and how the relationship you have with yourself affects every other relationship in your life.

Your Sense of Self-Worth Sets Your Standards

If you don’t like or love yourself, you won’t value yourself. Low self-worth leads to low standards — you accept behavior you shouldn’t because you don’t see your worth.

Pay attention to:

  • What you tolerate from others
  • How you speak to yourself
  • How you care for yourself

Treat yourself the way you treat someone you truly value. Set healthy boundaries and choose to give yourself what you need instead of always going without.

Your Self-Care Shapes Your Well-Being

Lack of self-care is self-neglect. When you neglect yourself, you bring a drained version of yourself into relationships. This creates unhealthy dynamics where your partner feels pressured to “rescue” you.

Self-care is not selfish. It is necessary for your happiness and for the health of your relationships. You deserve care, rest, and support from yourself.

Others Cannot Fill the Void You Create

When we don’t give ourselves love, attention, or reassurance, we desperately seek it from others. But no one can fill a void created by our own self-neglect.

This leads to:

  • Not believing compliments
  • Not trusting love from others
  • Feeling unloved even when someone cares
  • Fear-based relationships

Another person cannot reach your inner world the way you can — only you can give yourself the deep emotional care you need.

You Must Be Emotionally Safe for Yourself

Emotional safety means being able to express your feelings honestly without fear, shame, or judgment. When you ignore your own feelings or deny your needs, you are not emotionally safe for yourself.

If you cannot be open and vulnerable with yourself, you cannot be open and vulnerable with someone else. This blocks intimacy and limits the depth of your relationships.

You Co-Create Your Relationships

Relationships don’t just happen to us — we help create them. And the relationship you have with yourself guides every other relationship in your life.

You don’t need to be “perfectly healed” to love or be loved. You can learn self-love inside a relationship or outside of one. As you change, your relationships can change too.

The important part is recognizing that you have the power to choose how you treat yourself from this moment forward.

You Have a Choice

Will you keep neglecting, judging, or rejecting yourself? Or are you ready to change your life by changing your relationship with yourself?

Say “yes” to love — Say “yes” to self-love — Because it truly does change everything.
author: Marlena Tillhon

title: How do you value your self-esteem and self-worth?
header: Find Out How Valuing Yourself Leads to Better Choices and Happier Living
content:
Take a moment and think about someone you love who brings you joy. What thoughts come to mind? What do you love about this person — their humor, kindness, work ethic, intelligence? How much do you value them?

Now, think about yourself and ask the same questions:

  • What thoughts come to mind?
  • Do they make you feel good?
  • What do you like about yourself?
  • How much do you value yourself?

People who value themselves tend to make healthier choices and live more fulfilling lives. But many people struggle with self-worth and self-esteem. The good news: you can learn to see yourself more positively.

Self-worth and self-esteem

These terms are related, but not the same. Self-worth is your deep belief that you are good enough and worthy of love, respect and kindness. It is shaped by early experiences, discrimination, trauma, pressure to succeed, or chronic health conditions.

Self-esteem is more situational. It can shift after events like a breakup, losing a job, or receiving criticism. These experiences can make you doubt yourself.

Signs of low self-worth or low self-esteem include:

  • Criticizing yourself often
  • Making hurtful jokes about yourself
  • Focusing only on your mistakes
  • Believing others are better than you
  • Dismissing praise or compliments
  • Fearing failure and avoiding new things
  • Not caring for your appearance — or trying to look “perfect”
  • Feeling hopeless, ashamed, sad or worthless

Without healthy self-worth, you may avoid opportunities and stay in unhealthy relationships. Over time, this can lead to anxiety, depression, social phobia, ADHD, substance use and eating disorders.

Finding value in yourself

People with strong self-worth tend to have better self-esteem. They understand their strengths and weaknesses and face challenges with resilience — without feeling arrogant or selfish.

Here are simple ways to build a healthier sense of self-worth.

1. Challenge negative beliefs and thoughts

Negative beliefs usually come from repeated messages from parents, teachers, peers, or media. These messages are not facts.

When a negative thought appears, ask yourself:

  • Why do I believe this?
  • Is there evidence that it’s not true?
  • Is there another way to see this?
  • Would I say this to a close friend?
  • Am I being fair to myself?
  • If part of it is true, what can I learn from it?

2. Be kind to yourself

Treat yourself the way you treat someone you care about. Avoid comparing yourself to others — everyone has their own path.

Celebrate your wins. Do things you enjoy. When things don’t go as planned, learn from them without being harsh. No one is perfect. Allow yourself to make mistakes.

3. Be more positive

Try to intentionally think positive thoughts. This helps weaken negative patterns over time. Each day, think of 3 things you’re grateful for and write them down.

When negative thoughts appear, replace them with realistic and encouraging ones. Example: “I’m terrible at football” → “I’m improving, I work hard, and I enjoy playing.”

4. Empower yourself

A negative thought is just a thought — not a fact. Imagine sorting your mind like an inbox: delete the “spam” thoughts.

Reduce time with people or situations that trigger negative feelings about yourself. Say “no thank you” when needed. Choose people and places that make you feel appreciated.

5. Take care of yourself

Support your body and mind by eating nutritious food, getting enough sleep, staying active and connecting with others. Also, make time to relax and enjoy life.

title: Important life lessons we are often taught too late
header: Explore the Simple Morning Habit That Supports Digestion, Energy, and Wellness
content:
Important Life Lessons We Often Learn Too Late

Life is a long journey of learning. We rise and fall, succeed and fail, and collect lessons along the way. Some lessons come from books and advice, but many can only be understood through real experiences.

Here are some of the most important life lessons people often learn the hard way.

1. Walk Your Own Path

People will judge you and try to influence your choices. Do not let others push you away from your dreams. Follow your own path. It’s your life, your future, and your journey.

2. Don’t Hesitate When You Should Act

“Carpe diem” — seize the day. Many people miss chances because they lack courage. When you feel it's time to act, take action. No matter the result, you will learn something valuable.

3. Experience What You Learn

Reading and learning are helpful, but practice is what truly teaches you. You only understand something fully when you try it yourself.

4. Good Things Don’t Come Easy

A good life, strong career, and close relationships all require effort. Luck can only help a little. The rest depends on your hard work and willingness to learn from mistakes.

5. Never Stop Trying

Even if you give your best, you may still fail sometimes. Failure is not a sign to quit. It is a sign to try again with more wisdom and strength. Results come with persistence.

6. Take Care of Your Health Early

When you’re young, you can push your body hard. But unhealthy habits will affect you later. Start taking care of yourself now—eat well, sleep well, avoid harmful habits, and go for checkups.

7. Make Every Moment Count

Time goes faster than we think. Your twenties pass, then your thirties arrive in a blink. Do the things you want to do. Live fully, because tomorrow is never promised.

8. Live and Let Live

Trying to “fix” people can lead to conflicts. Do not force your ideas on others. Help them when they are ready and when they ask. Sometimes it’s better to step back.

9. Be Flexible With Your Goals

Plans may not always work at the time you expect. Sometimes you need to pause, adjust, or change your goal. Being flexible can save you from bigger problems.

10. Every Action Has a Reaction

Think before you speak or act. Even good intentions can hurt someone if they are not ready. Words and actions have consequences, so choose them wisely.

Use these lessons as guidance, not strict rules. Your life is unique, and only you know what is best for you. Enjoy your life and learn as you go.
